strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: generating compositional, interactive 3D scenes with independent, high-fidelity assets rather than monolithic fused meshes.

Proposes a coherent generate-then-compose pipeline that combines 2D generative editing, image-to-3D reconstruction, part-based spatial guidance, robust registration, SDF-based collision optimization, and VLM-driven refinement.
The SDF-based collision-aware optimization and the VLM agentic refinement are practical ideas that go beyond naive rigid registration and explicitly target physical plausibility.
Introduces a potentially useful large-scale interactive 3D dataset with over 8,000 compositional pairs and released poses, which could support future research if properly documented.
Reports improved CLIP alignment scores and lower surface/volume intersection rates compared with several baselines on the presented test set.
weaknesses: Experimental validation is very limited: only 10 test cases are used, with no variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance, and the quantitative metrics are insufficient to establish broad effectiveness.

No ablation studies are provided for the core components, including global-to-local registration, SDF-based collision optimization, and VLM-based agentic refinement. This makes it impossible to attribute the reported improvements to specific contributions.

The work lacks comparison with recent relevant compositional/part-generation methods such as OmniPart and SAM3D, and it does not benchmark against modern 3D-aware composition pipelines beyond fairly weak or inapplicable baselines.

The claimed dataset contribution is underdeveloped: curation details, quality control, filtering, licensing, annotation protocol, and dataset statistics are largely absent, and no benchmark or baseline is trained/evaluated on it.

Reproducibility is questionable due to heavy reliance on proprietary or rapidly changing external models (Nano Banana Pro/Gemini, TRELLIS2, PartField, GeoTransformer). Model versions, prompts, API settings, and costs are not specified, so code release alone may not make the pipeline reproducible.

The method description is incomplete in key places: the agentic refinement loop lacks concrete prompt templates, VLM details, stopping criteria, and failure handling; the SDF optimization is missing implementation details, runtime, and sensitivity analysis.

The evaluation does not validate physical soundness or interactivity beyond geometric intersection rates. No physics simulation, contact stability, manipulation success, or downstream robotic task is reported, despite motivation from Sim2Real and interactive scenes.

Clarity and notation need improvement: there are inconsistent primes in Table 1 and the text (e.g., M' vs. M_comp'), typos such as 'collsion', ambiguous equations/brackets, and several figures are too small or insufficiently described for a reader to verify the claims.

The 'PartField' baseline is marked as not applicable for CLIP metrics even though a composition result is produced and could likely be evaluated semantically; this weakens the quantitative comparison.

strengths: Targets a timely and relevant problem: compositional 3D generation with object-object spatial relationships and collision-awareness for simulation/robotics.

The generate-then-compose formulation is practical and training-free, exploiting strong off-the-shelf image/3D generative models (Nano Banana Pro/Gemini, TRELLIS2) and segmentation (PartField) as spatial priors.

The two-stage composition design is sensible: global-to-local registration (OBB + GeoTransformer + scale-aware ICP) for anchoring, followed by SDF-based collision-aware optimization for remaining parts.
The VLM-in-the-loop agentic refinement is an interesting idea for correcting severe occlusion-induced geometric mismatches that pose optimization alone cannot fix.

The qualitative examples and multi-view renderings suggest the pipeline can produce plausible compositions in some everyday cases; the proposed 8k-pair dataset, if released with documentation, could be useful.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is largely a pipeline integrating existing models plus classical ICP/registration and a straightforward SDF penalty; no new learned model, representation, or fundamental algorithmic advance.
Evaluation is far too narrow: only 10 test cases, no confidence intervals or statistical tests, and no human study. Claims of 'extensive experiments' are not supported.

Metrics are weak for the claims: CLIP measures 2D semantic similarity, not 3D object-object relations; intersection ratios measure only interpenetration, not physical stability, support/contact, gravity, affordances, articulation, or whether objects float.

Missing direct baselines: Copy-Transform-Paste and recent part-generation/inpainting methods (OmniPart, SAM3D, Hunyuan3D/Rodin-style segmentation/inpainting) are discussed but not quantitatively compared. Jigsaw and 2BY2 are from different tasks and may not be fair or sufficiently tuned.

Physical plausibility is overclaimed. The method does not model dynamics, materials, friction, mass, support surfaces, or interaction affordances, despite motivating robotic manipulation and Sim2Real.

The dataset contribution is under-substantiated: no construction protocol, filtering, validation, splits, task annotations, licensing, or quality analysis. If generated by the same pipeline, it may inherit the same errors and is not shown to be useful.
Reproducibility is concerning: heavy reliance on proprietary APIs (Nano Banana Pro/Gemini 3 Pro, TRELLIS2) with no prompts, versions, code, or compute details; dataset not linked.

Agentic refinement is largely qualitative: no quantitative ablation of its effect, iteration cost, failure modes, or comparison to simpler correction strategies; it may propagate errors and is capped at 5 iterations.
Sequential multi-part composition can compound errors; SDF collision loss is only against the anchor at each step, not simultaneous mutual collision handling across all objects.
Problem setup/abstract mismatch: the abstract motivates generation from single images under occlusion, but the actual pipeline requires a user-provided 3D mesh and text prompt.

Presentation issues: typos ('collsion'), broken figure/table formatting, notation inconsistencies (M', Mcomp, M'comp), equation 2 appears to have a bracket error, and some references/names (Nano Banana Pro vs Gemini) are unclear.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: compositional 3D generation for interactive scenes, with a training-free method that avoids requiring large-scale 3D compositional training data.

The proposed generate-then-compose pipeline is modular and technically sensible: it uses 2D/3D generative priors for guidance, PartField for coarse spatial cues, global-to-local registration for anchor alignment, SDF-based optimization for collision-aware placement, and VLM-driven refinement for severe mismatches.
Qualitative results are extensive and often compelling: two-part and multi-part compositions, multi-view renderings, and failure cases are shown, with clear visual improvements over baselines.

Quantitative comparisons report improvements in CLIP-based semantic alignment and in surface/volume intersection rates, supporting the claim that the method produces more collision-aware compositions.
The dataset contribution, with over 8,000 interactive pairs, could be useful for future work in structured 3D scene generation and robotic simulation.
The paper is generally clear, and the authors include meaningful discussions of limitations and failure cases, as well as a promise to release code.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation is limited: only 10 test cases, no standard benchmark, no statistical significance testing, and relatively small absolute gains in CLIP scores. The evidence is not yet strong enough to fully support broad claims of state-of-the-art compositional generation.

There are no proper ablations. The individual contributions of global-to-local registration, SDF-based collision optimization, and VLM-based agentic refinement are not quantitatively isolated, so the importance of each component is unclear.

The paper lacks a direct metric for spatial relationship / object-object alignment accuracy. Lower intersection rates can be achieved by simply pushing objects apart, so collision metrics alone do not prove that the intended guidance composition is preserved. Pose error or Chamfer distance against the 3D guidance scene would be more informative.

The method depends heavily on proprietary or externally hosted models (e.g., Nano Banana Pro, Gemini 3 Pro, TRELLIS2, PartField). This limits reproducibility and long-term accessibility, even if code is released.

The terms 'interactive' and 'physically-sound' are somewhat overclaimed. The method produces static, collision-free compositions, but does not evaluate physical stability, articulation, affordances, or downstream robotic interaction.

Dataset curation and quality control are insufficiently described. It is unclear how many generated scenes were filtered out, what constitutes a successful pair, and whether licensing or attribution issues arise from synthetic data generation.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair or incomplete. Jigsaw and 2BY2 are not directly designed for this setting, 2BY2 is retrained from scratch, and closely related methods such as COPY-TRANSFORM-PASTE are discussed but not compared.

strengths: Proposes a training-free generate-then-compose framework that combines 2D generative priors, image-conditioned 3D reconstruction, part segmentation, and registration for compositional 3D object generation.

Introduces a two-stage composition pipeline: global-to-local registration with GeoTransformer and scale-aware ICP for anchoring, followed by SDF-based collision-aware optimization that explicitly penalizes interpenetration.

Adds a VLM-driven agentic refinement loop to handle severe geometric mismatches that cannot be resolved by rigid transformation alone, and demonstrates extension to more than two objects via sequential composition.
Curates and plans to release a large interactive 3D dataset with over 8,000 pairs, which could be a useful resource for structured scene generation and robotic simulation.

Quantitative and qualitative comparisons suggest improved semantic alignment, collision avoidance, and spatial plausibility over several baselines; ablations support the roles of global-to-local registration, SDF optimization, and agentic refinement.
Targets a relevant and challenging problem: generating physically plausible, spatially consistent compositional 3D assets rather than monolithic fused geometry.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on proprietary or black-box components (e.g., Nano Banana Pro, Gemini 3 Pro, TRELLIS2, PartField, GeoTransformer) makes the pipeline difficult to reproduce and raises concerns about long-term availability and fairness of comparison. Runtime, cost, and failure modes of these components are not reported.

Technical novelty is mostly an integration of existing models and standard techniques. The SDF collision penalty is conventional, and the agentic refinement is primarily a prompt-based loop; the paper does not provide a new algorithmic formulation or theoretical insight sufficient for a strong algorithms contribution.

There is a mismatch between the abstract motivation (generating compositional objects from single images under occlusions) and the actual input, which is a user-provided 3D mesh plus text prompt. The method is not evaluated on single-image-to-3D compositional generation as implied.

Evaluation is not sufficiently rigorous. Only 150 test cases are used; human and VLM rating protocols are unclear (participants, prompts, scales, inter-rater reliability); no confidence intervals or significance tests are provided; CLIP scores are weak proxies for 3D structure and texture fidelity.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair or insufficiently adapted: Jigsaw and 2BY2 are not designed for text-conditioned or scale-optimized composition, and recent relevant part-generation methods (e.g., OmniPart, SAM3D) are discussed but not quantitatively compared.

The appendix reports 140 additional cases with 29 failures (about 20.7%), including symmetry ambiguity and collision-induced divergence. This undercuts the claim that the method robustly produces physically sound compositions.

The dataset contribution is not fully validated: it is generated by the authors' own pipeline, lacks manual verification, and contains only spatial placements rather than physically meaningful interaction annotations. The term 'interactive' is therefore somewhat overstated.

Collision metrics remain nonzero (e.g., R_volume = 3.876e-3), yet the paper frequently claims 'physically sound' and 'collision-aware' compositions; no physics simulation or downstream robot task evaluation is provided.

Several implementation details are missing or vague, including how Equation (3) is optimized with the non-linear SDF term, how the VLM refinement prompt is constructed, how many cases invoke agentic refinement, and how often it succeeds or fails.
No explicit contribution type is declared. As an algorithms paper the novelty is limited; as a systems/dataset paper the validation and reproducibility evidence need to be substantially stronger.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: composing individual 3D assets into collision-aware interactive scenes for simulation and robotics.
The generate-then-compose pipeline is conceptually clear and training-free, leveraging strong off-the-shelf generative and 3D reconstruction models.
Combines registration, SDF-based collision optimization, and VLM-driven refinement in a reasonable engineering pipeline.
Provides qualitative results, a quantitative comparison, and an appendix ablation to support the design choices.
Claims to release a large interactive 3D dataset of ~8,300 pairs, which could be valuable if properly validated and documented.
Discusses failure cases, including symmetry ambiguity and occlusion-induced collisions.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core system is largely an integration of existing models (Nano Banana Pro, TRELLIS2, PartField, GeoTransformer, ICP, VLM/Gemini/Qwen) with a standard SDF penalty; the algorithm contribution is incremental.

Task definition is inconsistent: the abstract frames the problem as single-image compositional generation under occlusion, but the method requires a user-provided mesh and relies on rendering it, so the central single-image/occlusion claim is not actually addressed.

Reproducibility is weak: the pipeline depends heavily on proprietary/closed-source models and APIs, and key details such as prompts, model versions, seeds, and exact VLM/editing procedures are missing; code and dataset are only promised.

Method details are insufficient: PartField segmentation into two parts and correspondence to the original/complementary assets is not validated; anchor selection by projected area is heuristic; registration and SDF optimization formulations leave correspondence and optimization details unclear.

The collision formulation only penalizes points of the remaining mesh inside the anchor mesh; it does not enforce symmetric collision handling or self-collision, and signed distance fields are unreliable for non-watertight/user meshes.

Physical plausibility is overclaimed: the method is collision-aware, not physically sound; it lacks gravity, support, contact, stability, friction, articulation, or dynamics, so 'interactive' scenes are essentially static compositions.

The agentic refinement is poorly specified and not quantitatively analyzed: VLM feedback generation, cross-section rendering, iteration cost, success rate, convergence, and possible semantic drift are not sufficiently evaluated.

Experimental evaluation is weak: only 150 test cases are used; several baselines are not adapted fairly or are unsuitable for the exact task; no recent compositional 3D generation methods are compared; no error bars or significance tests are reported.
Human/VLM rating protocols are underspecified, raising concerns about bias and reliability; CLIP score improvements are small and may not support strong claims.
Dataset claims are not substantiated in the manuscript: construction, annotation, pose quality, splits, licensing, and validation are absent, and the dataset may inherit the pipeline's failure modes.
Admitted failure cases, such as symmetry-induced orientation errors and occlusion-induced interpenetration, directly affect the paper's core claims and are not solved.
Presentation clarity suffers from mismatches between claims and actual setup, and important implementation/ablation details are relegated to the appendix.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: compositional 3D generation of interactive objects with object-object spatial relationships and physical plausibility, going beyond single-object 3D generation.

The proposed training-free generate-then-compose framework is practical and well-motivated, leveraging 2D/3D generative priors and robust registration rather than relying on scarce compositional 3D training data.

The two-stage composition pipeline is technically sound: global-to-local registration anchors the primary object, while SDF-based collision-aware optimization explicitly penalizes interpenetration and reduces surface/volume intersection rates.

The VLM-based agentic refinement introduces a useful semantic correction loop for cases where pose optimization alone cannot resolve severe geometric mismatches; the ablation supports its contribution.
Extensive qualitative results demonstrate improved spatial alignment, geometric fidelity, and collision avoidance compared with feed-forward, segmentation, and RANSAC-based baselines.
The planned release of an 8,000+ interactive pair dataset could be a valuable resource for future work in compositional 3D generation and robotic simulation.
The limitations and failure cases are explicitly discussed, which is helpful for assessing the method’s scope.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is limited by heavy dependence on proprietary or potentially unavailable systems such as Nano Banana Pro, TRELLIS2, Gemini 3 Pro, PartField, and GeoTransformer, with unclear versioning and access conditions.
The quantitative evaluation is limited to 150 test cases, and multi-part composition is demonstrated only qualitatively despite being a key extensibility claim.

Several baselines are not directly comparable: Jigsaw and 2BY2 lack the same text/image conditioning, 2BY2 is retrained, and MIDI is trained on 3D-FRONT; newer compositional 3D generation methods are not quantitatively compared.
The dataset contribution is under-described: filtering criteria, human validation of object-object relations and physical plausibility, licensing, diversity, and annotation details are not provided.

Technical robustness concerns remain: PartField segmentation errors propagate into pose guidance, SDF optimization assumes a reasonable signed distance field for user-provided meshes, and the agentic loop offers no convergence guarantee.
Failure modes such as symmetry ambiguity, mesh holes from TRELLIS2, and collision-induced divergence are acknowledged but not fully solved.
No runtime, API cost, or computational feasibility analysis is provided, despite the pipeline involving multiple large generative models and iterative refinement.

Evaluation metrics rely on CLIP scores and subjective human/VLM ratings; details of the human study are missing, and there is no explicit metric for preserving the geometric fidelity of the user-provided mesh or complementary mesh beyond collision rates.
